Let \(c_i=\cos x_i\), so \(c_i\in[-1,1]\) and \(\sum c_i=0\). Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{10}\cos(3x_i)
=\sum_{i=1}^{10}(4c_i^3-3c_i)
=4\sum_{i=1}^{10}c_i^3,
\]
since \(\sum c_i=0\).

So we need maximize \(\sum c_i^3\) under \(\sum c_i=0\), \(c_i\in[-1,1]\).

Suppose \(p\) of the \(c_i\)'s are positive and \(q=10-p\) are negative. Let the positive sum be \(S\), so the negative magnitudes also sum to \(S\). For fixed \(p\) and \(S\), the maximum of the positive cubes occurs by making as many positive entries as possible equal to \(1\), and the negative cube penalty is minimized when the \(q\) negative magnitudes are equal. Thus, if \(S=k\) is an integer endpoint, the maximum is
\[
k-\frac{k^3}{(10-p)^2},
\]
where \(0\le k\le \min(p,10-p)\).

Checking the possible \(p\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc}
p&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8&9\\
\hline
\max\left(k-\frac{k^3}{(10-p)^2}\right)
&\frac{80}{81}&\frac{15}{8}&\frac{120}{49}&\frac94&\frac{48}{25}&\frac32&\frac{10}{9}&\frac34&0
\end{array}
\]
The largest value is \(\frac{120}{49}\), attained at \(p=3\), \(k=3\): three cosines equal \(1\) and seven cosines equal \(-\frac37\).

Therefore
\[
\max\sum_{i=1}^{10}\cos(3x_i)
=4\cdot\frac{120}{49}
=\boxed{\frac{480}{49}}.
\]

\(\boxed{\frac{480}{49}}\)
